title: Communication during a four-week build
excerpt: Agree who answers, which channel holds decisions, and what a same-day reply covers. On a four-week build, silence costs a day you cannot add back at the end.
alt: Crates of used books at an outdoor stall, titles facing out. The titles are easy to scan, which is the standard for a short project note.
caption: Titles facing out, so you can choose without a speech. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who should answer during a short build?
faqs.answer: Name one approver on the client side and one lead on the studio side. Others may comment earlier. Those two close the loop. A decision that lives only in a side chat should be copied back to the canonical thread the same day, or it did not happen.

faqs.question: What does a same-day response cover?
faqs.answer: It covers a reply before the end of the working hours you agreed, not a finished design the same afternoon. A useful reply is often one line: seen, blocked, or this request is outside the four weeks. If you will miss the window, say so before it closes and say what happens to the date.

faqs.question: How should feedback be written?
faqs.answer: Point at the section and say what a stranger still cannot do. Separate defects against the approved frames, which belong in the build, from new ideas, which go on a list you will not raid in the last week. One collected note beats a trail of messages that revise the revision.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Working with a design studio on a four-week build goes well when you agree, before week one, how you will talk, who answers, and what a same-day response covers. Silence costs more than a short note that says the work is on the hard screen. The date is short. A missing answer does not sit politely in the background. It removes a day you cannot grow back.

Write the rules in one note both sides can find. Then follow them on the boring days, so they still exist on the tense ones.

## Who answers

Name one approver on the client side and one lead on the studio side. Others may comment. Those two close the loop. If a question has no owner, it will be answered by whoever is most anxious, which is how contradictory direction gets into the file.

The approver has to be reachable inside the week. A four-week build cannot wait for a monthly board meeting. If the approver travels, name a deputy with real authority, not a deputy who must check everything. Write the dates they are out at kickoff, not as a surprise on day ten.

Decide which channel is canonical. One thread for decisions, whether that is email or a shared channel. Side chats can happen. A decision that lives only in a side chat did not happen. Copy the sentence back to the canonical thread the same day. Future you will not remember which window held the yes.

Say who may talk to whom. Stakeholders sending direct notes to an engineer, while the approver sends different notes to the designer, splits the project into two projects. Route feedback through the approver. Route build questions through the studio lead. The route feels slower for an hour and faster for the month.

Hanabi’s public line of work is design and build together, so the lead can answer both a type question and a template question. If your studio splits those roles, say which one replies about what. A founder should not have to guess which silence means “still designing” and which silence means “blocked on DNS.”

## What same-day means

Same-day means a response before the end of the working day you agreed, in the timezone you agreed. It does not mean the work is finished the same day. It means nobody wonders if the message landed.

A useful same-day reply is often one line. “Seen. We’ll have the homepage frames tomorrow.” “Blocked on the headline. If we don’t have it by Thursday, the hero ships with the sentence from the brief.” “This feedback adds a template. That’s outside the four weeks. Parking it.” Those lines keep the schedule honest.

Define the hours. Ten to six in one zone, weekdays, is a clear window. Messages that arrive at midnight get a reply the next working day, and the agreement should say so. Otherwise “same-day” becomes a contest of whoever writes latest.

Say what same-day does not cover. A full new direction. A legal review. A photoshoot. A migration of a shop. Those can be acknowledged the same day and scheduled honestly. Pretending they fit the afternoon is how the four weeks become fiction.

If someone will miss the window, they say so before it closes, with the time they will answer. A late reply that arrives as a pile of changes is more expensive than a late reply that says “tomorrow morning, and the build continues on the current frames until then.”

## A weekly shape that fits in four

A four-week build does not have room for a vague cadence. Pick a shape and protect it.

Week one is the spine: the goal, the templates in scope, the words you already have, and the visual direction on the key screen. The conversation is decisions, not a tour of references you could have sent earlier.

Week two is the rest of the key templates and the states that are easy to forget: empty, error, mobile nav, the form confirmation. Feedback from week one is already in, or explicitly deferred.

Week three is build on the agreed frames, with a staging link a person can click. The conversation shifts from taste to defects against the frames. New taste is a change request, not a bug.

Week four is content in the real templates, the form reaching a person, metadata, redirects if a site is being replaced, and a list of what will wait. The conversation is “does this match what we approved,” not “what if the company was different.”

Inside each week, a short written update beats a meeting that repeats the file. Meet when a decision needs a voice. Do not meet to watch someone scroll. If you do meet, end with the decisions typed into the canonical thread before everyone leaves.

## Notes that keep the work moving

Write feedback against the goal. Point at the section. Say what a stranger still cannot do. “The first screen does not say what the product is” is a note the studio can use. “Make it pop” spends a day and returns the same argument. Nielsen Norman Group’s 2011 article on [how long users stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the reason that note matters: people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds is what earns more time. Week-one feedback should ask whether a stranger can tell what this is. It should not ask the team to be entertained.

Separate defects from ideas. A defect is “the button does not match the label we approved” or “the form never arrives.” An idea is “what if we added a journal.” Defects belong in the four weeks. Ideas belong on a list you will not raid at 6 p.m. on Thursday of week four.

One note, not a trail of messages that revise the revision. Collect yourself, then send. If you need a day to collect, say you need a day, and say what the studio should keep building in the meantime. Defaulting to the last approved frame is the right default. Waiting with no default is a pause you did not mean to buy.

Questions from the studio deserve the same discipline. They should be specific, with a recommendation. “We can use the existing photography or commission none and design for type. We recommend type, given the files in the drive. Need a yes by Wednesday.” A question with no recommendation invites a committee. A question with a deadline can be answered.

Keep the tone plain. You are two teams trying to ship a site, not a brand performing responsiveness. Short and specific is respectful. Long and vague is how people start missing the real ask.

## Silence, blockers, and the hard screen

The hard screen is the one that is taking longer for a real reason: a messy state, a stubborn layout, a migration surprise. The right message is that it is the hard screen, what you are doing about it, and whether the date moves. Going quiet until it is beautiful makes the other side invent a story, usually a worse one.

Blockers should be named the day they appear. Missing copy, missing DNS access, a stakeholder who has not seen the direction, a vendor that will not issue a key. Name the blocker, the person who can remove it, and the date it hits the schedule. A blocker written down can be removed. A blocker saved as politeness will remove the launch instead.

If the studio is blocked on you, you do not get to be annoyed that the file looks unchanged. If you are blocked on the studio, you deserve the one-line status. Both directions are the same rule. The work that is moving should be visible. The work that is stuck should be named.

Do not use a status meeting as the first time a risk is spoken. The canonical thread is for risks on the day they are real. The meeting is for the decision the thread could not finish.

A same-day culture still allows deep work. Batch the pings. A studio that answers every message in four minutes and never finishes a template has optimized the wrong promise. The agreement should protect a block of time when the status is “building, next update at four,” which is a response, not a disappearance.

## The last week

By week four the channel should feel quieter and more concrete. Staging, a punch list, and yes or no. New stakeholders who arrive in week four get a demo of what is shipping, not a vote on the direction. If they must have a vote, the date moves, and someone says that out loud.

The punch list is defects against the agreed site. It is not a mood board. Each item has a page, a sentence, and an owner. Items that are ideas go to the parking lot with the other ideas. You can do them next month. You cannot do them in the DNS window without trading away a check you wanted.

End the build with a note on how you will talk after launch. Who watches the form. Who may ask for a small fix. What “small” means. A four-week project that ends in silence is how the site starts to drift on day two. The maintenance conversation can be short. It should exist.

When the site is up, you will want a way to show the work that a client can approve in public. [A case study structure clients can approve](/blog/a-case-study-structure-clients-can-approve) is the next piece. It is about agreeing what may be said before anyone is surprised by a draft.

If you want to see how finished work reads when the decisions were specific, browse [Hanabi’s selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The projects are the public record, which is a different artifact from the weekly thread, and it deserves its own agreement.
